title: Missouri's 6th Congressional District election, 2026 (open seat — Sam Graves retiring)
description: This is an open-seat race for Missouri's 6th Congressional District, which covers 33 counties stretching from the Missouri River at St. Joseph to the Mississippi River at Hannibal, including part of Kansas City's Northland. Incumbent Republican Rep. Sam Graves, who has held the seat since 2001 and chairs the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, announced his retirement in March 2026, igniting a competitive primary. Five Republicans and three Democrats are vying for their party's nomination in the August 4 primary, with the general election on November 3, 2026. The Republican primary has drawn national attention as a proxy fight between allies of President Donald Trump and the political network of longtime Graves strategist Jeff Roe, with conservative radio host Chris Stigall (endorsed by Graves) facing Kansas City Councilman Nathan Willett, veteran Jim Ingram, and other challengers.

candidates.name: Chris Stigall
candidates.summary: Chris Stigall is a nationally syndicated conservative talk radio host and former congressional staffer seeking the Republican nomination. He previously served as a field representative and deputy communications director for retiring Rep. Sam Graves, who has endorsed his candidacy. Stigall emphasizes agriculture policy, government waste reduction, and support for President Trump's agenda, and has pledged to seek a seat on the House Agriculture Committee.

candidates.name: Jim Ingram
candidates.summary: Jim Ingram is a U.S. Army veteran, retired small business owner, and the first Republican to file for the 6th district seat. He earned a business degree from Kansas State University through an ROTC scholarship and an MBA from Drury College, then served four years on active duty at Fort Leonard Wood. Ingram's career spans banking, utilities, and entrepreneurship, and he describes himself as a 'Republican, the party of Common Sense' candidate.

He filed on the final day of candidate filing and is a first-time candidate for Congress. candidates.name: Josh Smead
candidates.summary: Josh Smead is a licensed architect, small business owner, and first-time candidate seeking the Democratic nomination. Born in Harrisonburg, Virginia, he earned a BA in Art History from James Madison University and a Master of Architecture from Iowa State University. Smead co-owns Liberty Design Development with his wife and has worked on large-scale sports architecture projects including NFL and NBA facilities. He emphasizes infrastructure, healthcare access, public education funding, and rural investment.

candidates.summary: Scot Pondelick is a U.S. Army veteran and combat Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) specialist who served three tours in Iraq, seeking the Democratic nomination. His campaign emphasizes service to country, showing up for North Missouri, and rejecting PAC money. Pondelick frames the open-seat race as a critical opportunity to change the district's direction after 26 years of Republican control.

candidates.summary: Matt Levine is a 37-year-old Democratic candidate who works as a Lead Transportation Security Officer at Kansas City International Airport and as a part-time special needs educator in the Park Hill School District. He holds a BA in Mathematics from the University of Maine, an M.Ed in Secondary Education from Grand Canyon University, and an MS in Accounting and Finance from Southern New Hampshire University. Levine's campaign focuses on education, healthcare, economic opportunity for working families, and government transparency.

forecast.rationale: No public polling exists for this race (based_on_poll_count=0), so the forecast relies entirely on structural and contextual factors. Missouri's 6th District has a strong Republican lean (Cook PVI R+16); Rep. Sam Graves held the seat from 2001 to 2026, winning his last three elections with 69–73% of the vote. However, this is an open seat with a competitive five-way Republican primary (endorsed candidate Chris Stigall versus Kansas City Councilman Nathan Willett, veteran Jim Ingram, and others) and a three-way Democratic primary, both on August 4 — six weeks from now. The crowded GOP primary introduces intraparty uncertainty (potential factional fallout between Trump-aligned and Jeff Roe-network candidates), and the Democratic field, while less established, includes credible veteran candidates. Without any polls, there is no way to measure whether primary dynamics or candidate quality meaningfully shift the general-election baseline. The high historical GOP baseline supports a Likely Republican rating (roughly 80–94% win probability), but the absence of polling and the open-seat dynamics prevent a Safe Republican rating. Confidence is low due to complete lack of survey data, and the 17-point margin estimate is a central projection consistent with a reduced (but still substantial) GOP advantage in an open-seat environment.
